# Quick start on simulated data {#sec-quickstart}

This chapter runs the whole workflow on a simulated experiment where the true tastes are known. It
uses small settings, so it runs in about two minutes. The estimates are rougher than at
the paper's settings, but every step is the same.

```{r}
#| label: qs-setup
library(sconjoint)
```

## A simulated tax-plan experiment

`sc_states()` needs to know how the experiment drew its profiles, because the standard errors
average over the comparisons each respondent could have seen. The package knows two designs: those
of the paper's applications. The simulation therefore reuses the recorded tasks of the first 600
respondents in the tax experiment of @ballard2017structure and simulates new choices from tastes we
choose.

Each task compares two tax plans. A plan is coded by 16 features: a linear and a quadratic term of
the rate in each of six income brackets (`tax1_linear` is the lowest bracket, `tax6_linear` the
highest) and four contrasts for the displayed revenue category. The linear and quadratic terms are
polynomial codes of the rate, each with mean zero and variance one over the bracket's menu of rates.

```{r}
#| label: qs-design
ex <- sc_example_data("br")
n <- 600; n_tasks <- 8
X <- ex$data$d[seq_len(n * n_tasks), ]     # recorded plan A minus plan B
colnames(X) <- ex$data$feature_names
id <- rep(sprintf("r%03d", seq_len(n)), each = n_tasks)
dim(X)
```

The simulated respondents have two characteristics: a standardized age and a 0/1 indicator for
Democrats. On average they dislike higher rates on low incomes and mildly like higher rates on
high incomes. Democrats like a higher top rate more. One taste factor ($q = 1$) moves the bottom
rate, the top rate and the first revenue contrast together, and each respondent has a modest pull
toward plan A.

```{r}
#| label: qs-truth
set.seed(2026)
Z <- cbind(age = round(rnorm(n), 2), dem = rbinom(n, 1, 0.5))
rownames(Z) <- unique(id)
fn <- colnames(X)
b0 <- setNames(rep(0, 16), fn)              # baseline mean tastes
b0[paste0("tax", 1:6, "_linear")] <- c(-0.6, -0.5, -0.3, 0, 0.2, 0.3)
b0[paste0("revenue_helmert", 1:4)] <- c(0.2, 0.1, 0.1, -0.2)
shift <- setNames(rep(0, 16), fn)           # how mean tastes move with the covariates
shift[c("tax1_linear", "tax6_linear")] <- c(0.2, 0.5)
mu <- outer(rep(1, n), b0) + outer(Z[, "dem"] + 0.1 * Z[, "age"], shift)
L <- setNames(rep(0, 16), fn)               # the one taste factor
L[c("tax1_linear", "tax6_linear", "revenue_helmert1")] <- c(0.3, 0.5, 0.2)
beta <- mu + outer(rnorm(n), L)             # each respondent's tastes
side <- 0.1 + sqrt(0.2) * rnorm(n)          # position effect: kappa = 0.1, omega = 0.2
eta <- rowSums(X * beta[rep(seq_len(n), each = n_tasks), ]) + rep(side, each = n_tasks)
y <- rbinom(n * n_tasks, 1, plogis(eta))
mean(y)
```

## Step 1: the data

`sc_data()` collects the choices `y`, the coded differences `X` (first profile minus second), the
respondent ids, the covariates `Z`, and any grouping variables used to define subgroups. `design =
"br"` names the randomization law.

```{r}
#| label: qs-data
x <- sc_data(y, X, id, Z = Z, groups = data.frame(dem = Z[, "dem"]), design = "br",
             orientation = "y = 1 selects plan A; X = plan A minus plan B")
x
```

## Step 2: the fit

`sc_fit()` splits the respondents into folds (five by default) and fits the model once per fold,
each time on the other four folds. Each fit learns the covariate scaling, trains the network with
early stopping on a validation subset of its training respondents, refines the common parameters,
and scores the held-out respondents. The settings below are much smaller than the paper's: a small
network, one start, at most 100 epochs and small integration rules.

```{r}
#| label: qs-fit
small <- list(hidden = c(16L, 8L), seeds = 1L, control = list(max_epochs = 100L, patience = 5L),
              nodes = 256L, check_nodes = 512L, heldout_nodes = 512L)
fit1 <- do.call(sc_fit, c(list(x, q = 1), small))
fit2 <- do.call(sc_fit, c(list(x, q = 2), small))
```

## Step 3: the number of taste factors

`sc_select_rank()` compares the fits by how well they predict the choices of held-out respondents.
It moves from $q - 1$ to $q$ factors only when the gain is more than two standard errors.

```{r}
#| label: qs-rank
sc_select_rank(list(fit1, fit2))
```

The data were simulated with one factor, so we continue with `fit1`.

## Steps 4 and 5: fold states, saved and loaded

`sc_states()` computes, for each fold, everything the estimator needs: the fitted mean tastes of all
respondents, the common parameters, the held-out respondents' scores, and each held-out respondent's
information. The information is the slow part. Here it uses 20 simulated designs per respondent; the
paper used 250 to 300.

```{r}
#| label: qs-states
st <- sc_states(fit1, M = 20L, ny = 2L, info_nodes = 256L, score_nodes = 512L)
file <- tempfile(fileext = ".rds")
sc_save(st, file)
st <- sc_load(file)
st
```

## Steps 6 and 7: targets and estimates

A target names one quantity. `sc_mean()` is the average taste for a contrast, `sc_share()` the
share of respondents whose taste is positive, and `sc_difference()` the difference between two
means. `sc_estimate()` computes all of them at once.

```{r}
#| label: qs-estimate
targets <- list(
  sc_mean("top rate: mean", "tax6_linear"),
  sc_share("top rate: share positive", "tax6_linear"),
  sc_difference("top rate: Democrats minus others",
                sc_mean("top rate, Democrats", "tax6_linear", w = "dem"),
                sc_mean("top rate, others", "tax6_linear", w = function(g) g$dem == 0)))
est <- sc_estimate(st, targets)
est
```

Each row gives the corrected estimate, the uncorrected fitted value (`plug_in`), the standard error,
a 95% interval, the interval rule, and the number of respondents the target averages over. Because
we simulated the data, we can compare the estimates with the truth in this sample:

```{r}
#| label: qs-compare
dem <- Z[, "dem"] == 1
truth <- c(mean(mu[, "tax6_linear"]),
           mean(pnorm(mu[, "tax6_linear"] / L[["tax6_linear"]])),
           mean(mu[dem, "tax6_linear"]) - mean(mu[!dem, "tax6_linear"]))
data.frame(target = est$name, truth = round(truth, 3), estimate = round(est$estimate, 3),
           lower = round(est$lower, 3), upper = round(est$upper, 3))
```

The true share uses the normal law of tastes: a respondent with mean taste $m$ and taste spread $s$
has a positive taste with probability $\Phi(m / s)$. The same calculation, applied to the fitted
law, is what `sc_share()` estimates.

## What to try next

@sec-gs and @sec-br apply the same steps to the paper's data, starting from the saved fits.
@sec-quantities lists every target. Data from another experiment go into `sc_data()`.
`sc_fit()` works for any design. `sc_states()` (and so `sc_estimate()`) currently supports only
the two built-in designs.
